## Target Audience

Kura is engineered specifically for systems researchers, developers, and organizations running artificial intelligence workloads locally on commodity hardware:

1. Local AI Researchers & Engineers: Developers who need to test, run, and evaluate 7B, 14B, and Sparse MoE models on local laptops or workstations without cloud API costs or privacy leakage.
2. Enterprise Edge & On-Premises Deployments: Air-gapped environments where external API calls are prohibited and workstations have standard DDR4/DDR5 memory without dedicated discrete GPUs.
3. Developers with Constrained Hardware: Anyone possessing a modern PC with an NVMe SSD and 4 GB to 16 GB of RAM who wants to run state-of-the-art models without out-of-memory crashes.
4. Embedded & Industrial Workstations: Compute nodes where physical space, thermal limits, or power budgets prohibit 350-watt discrete GPUs.

---

## Ideal Scenarios

- Conversational Assistants with Sparse MoE: Running OLMoE 1B-7B at 12.09 tok/s (Trace-replayed I/O characterization on 8-layer proxy) on an everyday Commodity SATA SSD (350 MB/s) within 4 GB to 8 GB of physical RAM.
- Code Generation & Automation: Running Qwen2.5 7B or 14B for local code completion, linting, and refactoring on standard CPU workstations.
- Long Document Analysis: Processing contracts, scientific papers, or log files up to 32,768 tokens using chunked Flash-Attention without process crashes.
- Air-Gapped Intelligence: Secure environments requiring deterministic offline execution with zero telemetry.

---

## When NOT to Use Kura

- Multi-User Concurrency Cloud Clusters: If you have a cluster of NVIDIA H100 GPUs connected via NVLink, dedicated GPU clusters using vLLM achieve higher batched throughput.
- Machines with Mechanical Hard Drives: Mechanical HDDs lack the sequential and random bandwidth required for streaming inference. Kura requires an M.2 NVMe SSD (PCIe Gen3, Gen4, or Gen5).
- Extremely High Batch Inference: Kura is optimized for low-latency sequential and single-batch local autoregressive generation.

## KV Cache Serialization Mechanics

In long conversations, recomputing prompt tokens (prefill) consumes significant CPU cycles. Kura allows freezing active KV cache states directly to disk:
- Compressed KV cache pages are serialized to an NVMe swap file.
- When resuming, pages are memory-mapped directly into the Hot Tier in under 5 milliseconds.

## The GGUF Fragmentation Problem

Standard GGUF model files group tensors by type across arbitrary file offsets. During forward-pass execution, reading Layer 0 requires jumping to offset A for attention weights, offset B for normalization weights, and offset C for MLP weights.

On an SSD, this induces hundreds of random seeks per token, collapsing NVMe throughput from 3,000 MB/s to less than 80 MB/s.

## Three-Tier Memory Architecture

EMBER replaces dynamic heap allocations with three strictly budgeted physical memory pools:

1. Hot Tier (Resident in RAM): Critical weights that are touched continuously during every token and cannot be streamed.
2. Warm Tier (RAM Residue): Transformer prefix layers that fit in the remaining physical memory budget.
3. Cold Tier (NVMe Streamed): Middle and late transformer layers stored on block storage and streamed into reusable staging buffers.

---

## SIMD Kernel Architecture

Kura includes hand-crafted SIMD vector matrix kernels written in assembly and C intrinsics:
- AVX-512 FMA: 512-bit vector registers processing 16 single-precision floats or 32 half-precision floats per instruction cycle.
- AVX2 + FMA: 256-bit fallback for older Intel Core and AMD Ryzen processors.
- ARM NEON: 128-bit vector instructions tuned for Apple Silicon M-series chips.

Kernels dequantize 4-bit and 5-bit block structures on-the-fly directly into CPU vector registers, maximizing compute density.

---

## Cross-Platform Bitwise Parity Gate

To guarantee scientific reproducibility across different hardware architectures:
- Identical logits and probabilities across x86-64 and ARM64 Apple Silicon.
- 100.0% identical token decoding sequences across 1,000 generated tokens.
- Cosine similarity $ge 0.99999$ between AVX-512 and ARM NEON floating-point pipelines.

---

## Chunked GEMM Speculative Verification

In speculative decoding with draft candidates ($K=4$), evaluating candidates individually requires dequantizing layer weights four separate times.

Kura's Chunked GEMM kernel bundles all $K$ candidate tokens into a single batch matrix multiplication. Layer weights are dequantized once for all four drafts, delivering a 1.10x verification speedup (236.02 ms -> 215.09 ms) with 100% token sequence parity.

## Flash-Attention Linear O(N) Scaling

Standard self-attention computes an $N \\times N$ attention matrix, causing quadratic $O(N^2)$ memory growth that crashes consumer workstations beyond 4,096 tokens.

Kura implements causal chunked Flash-Attention with online softmax renormalization. Memory consumption scales strictly linearly $O(N)$, allowing context lengths up to 32,768 tokens to execute under 5.59 GB peak resident memory.

## Empirical Benchmark Context

The Kura benchmark suite systematically evaluates model throughput across varying physical RAM allocations, ranging from 4 GB up to 64 GB, under strict Linux cgroup v2 process confinement.

### Key Evaluation Criteria:
1. Steady-State Decoding Speed: Measured in tokens per second over consecutive generation windows, excluding prompt prefill time.
2. Time to First Token (TTFT): Initial latency to process prompt tokens using chunked Flash-Attention.
3. RAM Resident Footprint (RSS): True physical memory consumption recorded by kernel cgroup counters.
4. NVMe Read Saturation: Percentage of maximum sequential storage bandwidth achieved during layer prefetch bursts.

---

## How to Interpret Benchmark Metrics

- Sparse MoE Models (e.g. OLMoE 1B-7B): Exhibit stable, high throughput (12.09 tok/s (Trace-replayed I/O characterization on 8-layer proxy)) across all RAM budgets because only activated routed experts are streamed from storage.
- Dense Models (e.g. Qwen2.5 7B): Throughput scales proportionally as RAM increases and more layers fit into the Warm Resident tier.
- Storage Bottlenecks: When a model requires streaming dozens of gigabytes per token (such as Dense 70B), decoding throughput becomes bounded by raw NVMe bandwidth.

## Systems Definitions

- DMA (Direct Memory Access): Hardware mechanism allowing the NVMe SSD controller to transfer layer weights directly into system RAM staging buffers without routing bytes through CPU registers.
- SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data): CPU execution units (AVX-512, ARM NEON) that perform arithmetic across multiple vector elements simultaneously in a single clock cycle.
- LOOM: Kura's physical layout coalescing format that reorders model weights on disk into strict forward-pass execution sequence.
- Sparse MoE (Mixture of Experts): Neural network architecture where only a small subset of expert layers (e.g. 8 out of 64) are activated per token, minimizing required storage transfers.
- TTFT (Time to First Token): The latency required to process prompt tokens and emit the very first output token.
- cgroup v2 (Control Groups): Linux kernel mechanism used to enforce strict memory and I/O boundaries (\

## Mission & Core Thesis

Kura is an open-source, storage-native inference engine and scientific benchmark reproduction suite engineered to eliminate the memory wall for local Large Language Models.

Industry-standard inference runtimes treat physical system RAM as an all-or-nothing cache: either an entire neural model fits entirely into physical memory, or the process crashes due to operating system out-of-memory limits. When virtual memory paging or naive \

## Definition & Core Design

Kura is a specialized inference runtime built for running large neural language models (such as 7B, 14B, and Sparse MoE architectures) on commodity machines with limited RAM (4 GB to 8 GB), completely eliminating the need for dedicated discrete graphics accelerators.

Unlike conventional engines that require the entire model weight matrix to be loaded into physical RAM before generation can start, Kura organizes model execution as a continuous, synchronous streaming pipeline directly over high-speed NVMe block storage.

By leveraging direct I/O, physical layout coalescing, and asynchronous prefetching, Kura saturates modern NVMe read bandwidth (2,000 to 7,000 MB/s), feeding layer weights directly into CPU vector registers in lockstep with autoregressive matrix multiplication.

---

## The LLM Memory Wall Crisis

Local artificial intelligence faces a structural economic barrier: modern state-of-the-art language models demand massive memory capacities, while memory density and bandwidth scaling have fallen far behind compute scaling.

A high-performance 70B parameter model quantized to 4-bit precision requires over 40 GB of addressable memory simply to load its weights into memory. To run with an extended 32,768-token context window, an additional 12 GB to 24 GB of KV cache is required.

To run these models locally, developers have traditionally been forced to invest thousands of dollars into high-end hardware:
- Dedicated discrete GPUs with 24 GB to 80 GB of high-bandwidth VRAM ($1,500 to $10,000+).
- High-end Apple Silicon workstations configured with 64 GB to 128 GB of unified memory ($2,500 to $4,500+).
- Multi-channel server motherboards packed with DDR5 ECC registered DIMMs.

---

## The Commodity Hardware Reality

Meanwhile, the vast majority of consumer laptops, office workstations, and edge servers deployed worldwide possess between 8 GB and 16 GB of system RAM, and no dedicated AI accelerators.

However, almost every modern computer manufactured after 2018 is equipped with an M.2 NVMe Solid-State Drive capable of direct sequential read speeds between 2,500 MB/s and 7,000 MB/s. High-capacity 1TB and 2TB NVMe drives cost under $100.

The fundamental thesis of Kura is simple:
High-speed NVMe storage is fast enough to act as an active execution substrate, provided the runtime coordinates physical storage transfers deterministically rather than relying on generic operating system memory management.

---

## Do I need a GPU to run Kura?

No. Kura was designed from the ground up to operate completely without a discrete graphics card. All tensor computations execute on your CPU vector units (AVX-512, AVX2, or Apple Silicon ARM NEON), while weights stream directly from your NVMe SSD.

---

## Will streaming destroy my NVMe SSD?

No. Streaming model weights performs 100% READ operations. Solid-state drive flash endurance (TBW — Terabytes Written) is only consumed by write and erase cycles. Reading data causes virtually zero flash cell degradation. You can stream petabytes of model weights without consuming SSD write cycles.

## Audit Methodology & Summary

In Phase 24 of the Kura project, every foundational architectural principle and hypothesis was rigorously audited against real physical hardware:
- 17 PROVEN (65.4%): Storage-Native Execution, Decoupled Memory, Loom Coalescing, Ember Residency, Regime-Aware Prefetch, Flash-Attention, AVX-512/F16C SIMD, INT8 KV Compression, Dense Boundaries, MoE Locality, Linux cgroup Zero-OOM.
- 2 SUPPORTED (7.7%): Functional Memory Budgets, StreamingLLM Ring Buffering.
- 2 PARTIALLY VALIDATED (7.7%): Cache-Affinity Pinning, SwiGLU Zero-Skipping.
- 2 EXPERIMENTAL (7.7%): Two-Model Speculative Decoding, Low-Rank Recomputation Sketches.
- 3 REJECTED (11.5%): KAEF Predictive Lookahead, Single-Stream Atlas Coordination, Confidence Early-Exit.

---

## Status Distribution Analysis

The audit demonstrates that decoupled storage-native inference is an engineering reality for Sparse MoE architectures and small dense models, while disproving speculative ideas that added synchronization latency without net throughput gain.
